title: No black box.
Just evidence.
intro: A verdict is only as useful as the method behind it. Follow the journey from public conversation to explainable insight—and see where the limits are.

stages.title: Collect
stages.detailTitle: Start with the conversation, not a conclusion.
stages.detail: VerdictLab accepts public Reddit and YouTube conversations, or an uploaded CSV / XLSX dataset. The source and available dates stay attached to the analysis so the results have context.

stages.title: Clean & protect
stages.detailTitle: Prepare the text without losing its trail.
stages.detail: Records are normalized for analysis and supported personal-information patterns are redacted before scoring. Original source references remain available for traceability.

stages.title: Score
stages.detailTitle: Read the same words three ways.
stages.detail: Concept-based, rule-based, and lexicon-based approaches each surface a different signal. No single model is treated as the final truth.

stages.title: Cross-check
stages.detailTitle: Agreement is a signal. Disagreement is a prompt.
stages.detail: Model outputs are compared side by side. Differences are retained so you can investigate ambiguity instead of having it averaged away.

stages.title: Explain
stages.detailTitle: The method travels with the verdict.
stages.detail: Explore the supporting records, model perspectives, and known limitations behind each summary before drawing a conclusion.

examples.label: Positive
examples.quote: “This is a great improvement. I really love the new design!”
examples.note: Educational sample · not a live prediction
examples.callout: Similar positive readings strengthen the signal. They do not guarantee a correct interpretation.

examples.label: Negative
examples.quote: “This update made everything slower and harder to use.”
examples.note: Educational sample · not a live prediction
examples.callout: Agreement can make a signal clearer, but context and sampling still determine what it means.

examples.label: Neutral
examples.quote: “The announcement is scheduled for Thursday at 10am.”
examples.note: Educational sample · not a live prediction
examples.callout: A neutral score describes the text signal, not the importance of the conversation.

examples.label: Sarcasm
examples.quote: “Fantastic, another redesign that fixes absolutely nothing.”
examples.note: Educational sample · not a live prediction
examples.callout: Sarcasm can reverse apparent meaning. Disagreement is a reason to inspect the original text.

models.name: SenticNet
models.description: Looks beyond individual words to connect concepts with sentiment and affective meaning.
models.limitation: Concept coverage matters. When concepts are unavailable, the uploaded pipeline can fall back to VADER. Hourglass emotion dimensions are exploratory, not validated emotion diagnoses.

models.name: VADER
models.description: A social-text specialist that accounts for emphasis, punctuation, negation, and sentiment-bearing words.
models.limitation: Its lexicon and rules provide an interpretable comparison baseline, but sarcasm, domain-specific language, and context can still mislead it.

models.name: TextBlob
models.description: Provides another perspective on polarity, helping reveal when different approaches read the same text differently.
models.limitation: Polarity runs from −1 to +1. Its language patterns and lexicon do not fully understand social context or subtle intent. Scores are not directly interchangeable across models.

trustPoints.title: Evidence before certainty
trustPoints.description: Read the supporting comments, sample context, and model differences—not just the headline verdict.

trustPoints.title: Privacy is part of the process
trustPoints.description: Supported personal-information patterns are redacted before scoring. Avoid uploading sensitive or private conversations.

trustPoints.title: Evaluation, not inflated claims
trustPoints.description: The project includes evaluation workflows with accuracy, macro-F1, and bootstrap intervals. This preview makes no unverified performance claim.

trustPoints.title: People stay in the loop
trustPoints.description: Use the results to explore conversation, not to diagnose people, make high-stakes decisions, or claim what the entire public believes.

faqs.question: Can VerdictLab understand sarcasm?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. Sarcasm can reverse the apparent meaning of positive words. Model disagreement can flag a reason to inspect the text, but all models can also agree and still be wrong.

faqs.question: Does “high confidence” mean the verdict is correct?
faqs.answer: No. Confidence is a heuristic based on sample size and model agreement. It is not a calibrated probability, an accuracy score, or proof that sampled opinions represent the public.

faqs.question: How is the methodology evaluated?
faqs.answer: The project includes an evaluation workflow for an independently labelled sentiment test set. It measures accuracy and macro-F1 with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Emotion dimensions are not validated by a sentiment benchmark.

faqs.question: What about Malay or mixed-language comments?
faqs.answer: The included tools are primarily English-oriented. Malay, code-switching, local slang, and multilingual conversations need separate validation. Treat results cautiously rather than assuming equivalent performance.

faqs.question: Is a public conversation the same as public opinion?
faqs.answer: No. A platform, community, collection window, and available sample all shape the result. A verdict describes the collected conversation, and it does not establish cause and effect.
